metadata.title: Introduction of multistage adaptive testing design in PISA 2018 (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper evaluates a multistage adaptive testing (MSAT) design for PISA 2018 Reading using a simulation study rather than estimating student achievement from the operational PISA microdata. Because the analysis is based on generated item responses and design-induced missingness (items not taken), the usual PISA complex survey weighting variables (e.g., student sampling weights and replicate weights) are not described as being applied. The routing and testlet assignment are governed by the MSAT algorithm (performance-group thresholds on automatically scored items and a probability layer matrix), not by survey-weighted estimation. For any future empirical implementation using PISA microdata, analysts should apply the standard PISA student sampling weights and replicate weights to account for the multistage sampling design and clustering; however, this paper’s reported results focus on measurement-model recovery and precision under the simulated MSAT mechanism.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the study is a simulation and evaluates MSAT performance via item-response-theory (IRT) parameter recovery and measurement precision (e.g., EAP-based reliability and Warm’s weighted likelihood standard errors), rather than producing PV-based achievement outcomes. Missing data handling is not reported in the sense of an imputation strategy because the “missingness” arises mechanically from the MSAT design (items not administered to a student), and the paper does not describe any additional missing-data imputation procedure. This is therefore a design-induced missingness setting rather than a conventional missing-data problem requiring an imputation method.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Simulation study: item responses are generated from a 245-item pool using preliminary PISA 2018 field-trial parameters, then MSAT routing is applied to convert unadministered items to missing. The simulation assumes 12 fictitious country groups with heterogeneous latent ability distributions; the paper does not provide per-country analytic sample sizes for these fictitious groups, and it does not report an empirical student analytic sample from operational PISA microdata.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates a multistage adaptive testing (MSAT) design implemented for the PISA 2018 main survey in the Reading domain. The MSAT administers three stages (Core, Stage 1, Stage 2) using testlets (units of items) and routes students based on performance on automatically scored items, grouped into low/medium/high using testlet-specific number-correct thresholds derived from test characteristic curves. Two routing designs are compared: Design A (Core > Stage 1 > Stage 2) administered to 75% of students and Design B (Core > Stage 2 > Stage 1) administered to 25% to mitigate potential position effects for Stage 2 items. Using a simulation with 245 dichotomous/polytomous items and IRT scaling via a multiple-group IRT model (2PL for dichotomous, GPCM for polytomous) estimated with marginal maximum likelihood, the MSAT design achieved parameter recovery comparable to the operational benchmark and improved measurement precision by about 4.5% on average, with gains up to ~10% at extreme proficiency levels. The study is based on a single simulated dataset, so additional simulation work is recommended to assess robustness (e.g., omission rates and item-by-country interactions).
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD technical report describing and evaluating an assessment design through simulation rather than an empirical ML prediction study on student-level outcomes. As a result, there is no ML model training/evaluation, no PV-based achievement target, and no reported survey-weight application or missing-data imputation strategy. The report also does not provide an operational analytic sample with per-country student counts; instead, it uses 12 fictitious country groups with a fixed simulated sample size per group (N=6,300) to study measurement-model recovery and precision under MSAT routing.
